title: Bram and Boots' Legendary Choice
markdown:
Craggy mountains scraped the sky. At night lanterns sat in the lanes like stars that had chosen to walk. The air smelled of pine and a rumour of snow.

Bram was an ogre. People expected grumble and stomp. He was gentle, steady, quiet, clever in the way that does not shout. His green hands could crush boulders and also spare the smallest alpine flower. His amber eyes missed little. Boots, a scruffy dog of no particular breed, smelled of damp earth and sunshine and walked in Bram’s shadow as if shadow were a job.

Village Lumina was near. Banners of pale cloth already hung between pines, waiting for lamps. Every household presented a familiar—friendship with a little gentle magic—to bless the season: a fox last year, a moth the year before, once a goat that had eaten the blessing and been forgiven. The rite was old as the tallest pines. Bram wanted something worthy, something that looked like respect when the Head Elder’s spectacles found it. He had walked the village imagining nods. Boots had walked it imagining sausages. Both plans had a kind of honesty.

“Boots,” he rumbled, stones in a soft stream. “A companion for the Lumina. Something legendary.” Boots thumped a tail against a boot, licked, and offered the kind of silence that meant: whatever you pick, I will still be here. Bram heard it. He still wanted a creature the elders would recognise as a story.

The Great Mountain Market waited over valleys of wildflowers and ridges where the wind practised old songs. They walked until Bram’s knees remembered every stone and Boots’s paws found every interesting smell and rejected most of them. A child waved; an old woman did not flinch at an ogre, which was a kindness Bram filed away. The market arrived as colour shouting, spices arguing with burnt sugar, damp wool, and a metallic tang that meant someone was selling courage in a cage. A goat wore a ribbon and looked ashamed. Steam rose from a pot that claimed to be stew and might have been a dare.

A merchant with a rusty-hinge voice offered a griffin chick, fist-sized, forged in Sky Peak winds, guaranteed brave. It cheeped and tried to eat its tail. “Courage is useful,” Bram said. “It looks wobbly. And hungry for itself.”

A shimmering cloak hid a miniature phoenix, forever reborn, flame for the path. Unfurled, it was a sleepy flicker that dozed and sighed. Bram touched the luck-stone in his pocket. “A light that naps is a stubbed toe waiting.” Boots’s ear agreed.

An imp on scrolls offered cosmic riddles. Bram asked how to mend a leaky roof so rain missed the favourite armchair. The imp blinked, slow. “No cosmic significance.” Bram’s sigh was dry leaves. Clever, and no use to furniture.

Frustration sat in his chest, tight as a badly tied parcel. He had pictured the elders’ nod, the lanterns approving, a creature that looked like a page from a proper book. Legendary, on these stalls, meant trouble in a prettier wrapper: courage that ate itself, light that snored, wisdom that would not mend a roof. Boots sniffed a mushroom that glowed like a shy lamp, then a stall of tiny carved animals—fox, hare, a very serious owl—and looked at Bram with the intelligence of someone who had already chosen and was waiting for the ogre to catch up. A clock somewhere struck a thin hour. The Lumina would not wait for the perfect roar.

They drifted from the noise as the sun went gold and long. In a quiet corner a stall wore grey linen. On a moss cushion sat a round charcoal fluff that seemed to drink sound. Amber eyes, soulful, still. A Shadow-Puff.

“Ordinary,” said the gnome vendor, silver bells in his beard jingling offence. “No roar. No prophecy. Barely a sound. You want thunder, Bram. Not fluff. It will impress no one.” A woman in a hat of too many feathers called that it had no sparkle.

The market’s taste felt like a shoe that had not been asked. Bram stood in it and felt large in the wrong way. The Puff’s stillness was a small room; he could have bought it and been kind, and still been performing. Then Boots nudged his elbow—not toward griffin or phoenix or fluff, toward something that had fallen from a toy stall into the dust beside an ogre’s careful foot: a wooden bird, wings true, body polished by patience, warm from the day’s handling. A child’s stall, prices in chalk. It fitted the palm as if the carver had known a larger hand would need it.

Boots whined softly, tail a slow wag that did not need a legend. He was not presenting a familiar. He was the familiar.

“You are the legend,” Bram whispered, low enough for fur. He straightened. “I have chosen.”

Not to the gnome. To the square, voice steady. “I choose Boots.”

Hush, then a weather of murmurs. A dog? Lineage? The Head Elder came, spectacles, brow like a forecast. “Affection is fine, Bram. Lumina wants lore. Power. Heritage.”

He held the wooden bird so the last light could find it, and looked at Boots, who sat as if dignity were a breed. “He has walked every path. He knows my weather before I do. He nudges when I need it and warns when I do not yet see. Loyalty like these mountains. That is more than a flame that sleeps or a roar for sale. He has always been my familiar.”

The Elder’s sternness thinned. She saw not a foolish ogre but a man who had finished a thought. “A companion of proven heart,” she said, “is a treasure.”

They walked home under rose and lavender, the wooden bird in Bram’s pocket knocking softly against the luck-stone as if the two objects had decided to be colleagues. Approval followed like a warmer wind; a spice-seller nodded who had earlier recommended thunder. At Lumina the lanterns woke on lanes and doors, one by one, like people remembering their names. Someone had hung pine above the well. Bram and Boots stood at the edge without a speech. Boots nudged his hand. Villagers who had come to be sceptical found themselves watching a bond that did not need a stall. A griffin chick, somewhere, was still eating its tail; nobody fetched it for the blessing. Night came in. Pine and woodsmoke did the rest. High on a ledge, snow took a few quiet pawprints and kept the secret. Bram did not call it magic. He called it Tuesday, and the best one.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
